books.section: Topic 4.12 African Americans in the Early Republic, B. The Cultures of African-American Communities

primary_sources: The North Star, first issue, December 3, 1847

stimulus.text:
"Brethren, arise, arise! Strike for your lives and liberties. Now is the day and the hour. . . . Rather die freemen than live to be slaves. Remember that you are FOUR MILLIONS!" — Henry Highland Garnet, "An Address to the Slaves of the United States," National Negro Convention, Buffalo, New York, August 1843.

"Right is of no Sex—Truth is of no Color—God is the Father of us all, and we are all brethren." — Motto of The North Star, Frederick Douglass’s newspaper, first issue, December 3, 1847.

The convention refused to endorse Garnet’s address, by a single vote, and Douglass spoke against it.
stimulus.source_note: Verbatim public-domain quotations: Henry Highland Garnet, “An Address to the Slaves of the United States,” National Negro Convention, Buffalo, August 1843; motto of The North Star, first issue, December 3, 1847. Wording checked against BlackPast and the Library of Congress.

source: original; stimuli are verbatim public-domain quotations from Garnet (1843) and The North Star (1847)
stem: The North Star’s motto best shows that Douglass’s paper stood for

options.text: colonization of free Black Americans in Liberia
equal rights for all people, regardless of sex or color
the right of states to decide slavery for themselves
options.misconception: The motto claims universal right and truth, not states’ rights.

options.text: an end to all newspapers run by white abolitionists
options.misconception: Douglass broke with Garrison’s paper but did not seek to end white papers.

rationales.A: Douglass opposed colonization. The motto claims rights for people where they are, not in Liberia.
rationales.B: Right is of no sex, truth is of no color, and God is the father of us all. One standard of rights for everyone.
rationales.C: The motto says nothing about states deciding slavery. It claims rights that belong to all people.
rationales.D: Douglass founded his own paper after breaking with Garrison, but he never sought to end white abolitionist papers.
rationales.general:
1. Read the motto word by word. Right is of no sex; truth is of no color; God is the father of us all.
2. Ask what it rules out. No right depends on being male or white.
3. Name the stand. One standard of rights for everyone.
Background: Douglass founded the North Star in Rochester, New York, in December 1847.
Remember: a motto is a promise in one line; test it against what the paper did.
